title: Hearing Fletcher Henderson at the Chicago Armory
summary: He names every member of Henderson's band, from Hawkins and Buster Bailey to Tommy Ladnier, and meets them during the week Tunney beat Dempsey.

story.theme_name: Who was in the band: naming sidemen and personnel
story.community_name: Who played in the band: reciting personnel

blocks.x: And we got to Chicago. And the Chicago Defender, they gave us free tickets to go to that affair. And Doc, I was the happiest person in the world, because I had all my life -- see, Fletcher Henderson's band was the hottest band out at that time, see. His band had been hot from the early 20's on up when he made "Sugarfoot Stomp." That was when Louis Armstrong was playing with him, and he made that famous recording -- Fletcher Henderson -- the "Sugarfoot Stomp." That was the piece that introduced him to America, "Sugarfoot Stomp."
Okay. Fletcher Henderson. We all went down to the Chicago Armory. I can name every member of that band right now.

His reed section was Buster Bailey on alto sax and clarinet. He had Jerome Pascual playing alto sax and clarinet. Coleman Hawkins played the tenor saxophone. Trumpet -- he had Russell Smith playing first trumpet. Joe Smith was playing second trumpet, and a fellow named Tommy Ladnier playing third trumpet and he was the get off man.

Tommy Ladnier. He was a hot trumpet player out of New York at that time. On trombone he had a fellow named Moten. I just can't think of Moten's first name, but Moten played a beautiful trombone. In later years Moten made the original "One O'Clock Jump" with Count Basie. And he played the original -- the first solo played on "One O'Clock Jump" Moten played that with the Count Basie Band.
This is no relation to Bennie Moten?

No. No relation at all. And Jimmy Harrison Hash, trombone. Jimmy Hash was from Louisville, Kentucky. Great trombonist. He died young. On drums he had a fellow named Kaiser. Kaiser was the one that introduced the hand cymbal. Just played drums and used to have a hand cymbal, and you could play them with sticks. You know, he introduced that effect, the hand cymbal effect.
That was the -- the bass player -- I can't remember his name. But the rest of those fellows -- and I met them all, and I talked with them, and I got to be a great friend of
Buster BAiley and a great friend of Coleman Hawkins before he died.

But that trip, that was a great trip. And I shall never forget it because that was the week that Tunney beat Dempsey in Chicago. Chicago was Chicago then. That was when South Parkway was South Parkway, a beautiful street. And as you got along where the parks were, they had the tennis courts all the way up to 60 -- to 60th Street, I think it was. That was 1927.
